summary:
Karnātaka stands under India's national framework for transgender recognition and protection. The operative baseline for a trans visitor is the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill passed by both houses of India's Parliament in March 2026, which narrows the 2019 Act it amends. Presidential assent remained pending as of late March 2026.

The amendment removes the self-identification route to legal recognition established under the 2019 law and reverses the recognition principle set by the Supreme Court in 2014. Recognition is now restricted to persons belonging to traditionally or historically recognised socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex persons, with eligibility assessed on biological or physical traits alongside those traditional identities. Self-identified trans men, trans women and non-binary people who fall outside those categories are outside the recognition scheme.

Recognition also requires medical certification. Under the amended law, medical boards and district authorities must certify that gender-affirming surgery has taken place before identity recognition is granted, replacing the declaration-based route that the 2019 Act provided.

The bill adds offences, including a penalty of up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring anyone to be transgender. Human Rights Watch stated on 26 March 2026 that this provision risks criminalising the support networks that trans people rely on.

Identity documents remain a practical constraint. India's census records 487,803 transgender persons, of whom only about 32,500 hold identity cards, so most trans people in the country cannot present an official document matching their gender identity at checkpoints, airports or police stations.

The government presents the narrower definition as targeting welfare benefits and anti-trafficking protection more precisely. Critics, among them rights organisations, warn that it excludes many trans men, trans women and non-binary people from legal recognition altogether. India is estimated to have around two million transgender people.

Entry and stay sit alongside a mixed protection baseline. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which courts have interpreted to cover gender identity, while no same-sex marriage or civil partnership is available. Criminal-law protection weakened with the replacement of the Indian Penal Code by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita in 2024, which dropped gender-identity-specific offences against sexual violence that the previous code carried.
tangentialFactors:
The amendment is under active institutional contest. A Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel asked the government to withdraw the bill, describing the removal of self-identification as a setback against the court's 2014 ruling, and Human Rights Watch urged the president not to sign it. The measure's final legal status therefore turns on an assent decision that was unresolved at the end of March 2026.

Assessments of official conduct toward trans people diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic, while victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. Documented checkpoint friction includes the November 2024 stop of openly transgender law student Sakshi Jain at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite her PAN card, and a February 2026 Allahabad High Court grant of relief to a trans person required by passport authorities to undergo a medical examination.

The Madras High Court judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. Bans issued from that judgment and by the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.
localsOnly:
Residents seeking recognition must now satisfy medical boards and district authorities rather than make a statutory declaration, and the range of qualifying identities has narrowed to traditionally recognised groups and intersex persons. Trans people outside those categories have no route to a corrected identity document under the amended scheme.

The government frames the narrower definition as sharpening the targeting of welfare benefits and of protection from trafficking. States including Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha run transgender welfare boards coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions, and several states provide targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits for hijras. Nationally, the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community, and in August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.

The 32,500 identity cards issued against a census count of 487,803 transgender persons indicate that the overwhelming majority of residents carry no document evidencing their gender identity. Intersex residents remain exposed to non-consensual surgery in infancy: reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male, and the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.

Activists including Akkai Padmashali describe the amendment as criminalising and as an attack on the right to exist, while rights groups contest its exclusion of trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people from recognition.
outOfScopeNotes:
Presidential assent to the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill was pending as of late March 2026; whether it has since been signed, amended or judicially challenged is not sourced here.

No Karnataka-specific enforcement data appears in this inventory: state-level police practice, the availability of a Karnataka transgender welfare board, and any state schemes or High Court rulings of Karnataka are unresolved and not sourced.

Human Rights Watch's statement that the new coercion offence could criminalise support networks is an assessment of risk rather than a documented prosecution; no case brought under that provision is sourced.

The figure of around two million transgender people nationally is an estimate, and the census count of 487,803 records only persons who were enumerated as such.

Whether medical boards and district authorities apply the certification requirement consistently across states, and how the amendment interacts with earlier Supreme Court directions on self-identification, remain unresolved on this record.
